modalLead: A monitored bookmark's statistics can now be opened at full size. The row had room for a 24-hour uptime figure and one ping, while the rest — 7-day and 30-day uptime, the check counts, the outage list — was already there and never shown. Press ⤢ on the row, or i, for a large response-time chart and the whole picture, without losing your place in the list.

items.text: Enlarge a monitored row's statistics — the ⤢ button at the end of the monitor strip opens a large response-time chart with min, average and max marked and a tooltip on every point, plus uptime for 24 hours / 7 days / 30 days side by side with the number of checks behind each, a taller heartbeat bar, the check interval and last check time, and the full outage list. It opens instantly: it shows the report already on screen rather than fetching anything new.

A window with no data says so — uptime over 30 days is left as no data rather than 0% when there are no samples yet. A monitor you switched on an hour ago has no month of history, and showing that as total downtime would read as an outage that never happened.

i opens it from the keyboard — added to the shortcut legend under the feed next to s, p, c and m. Esc closes the statistics and leaves the health view exactly where you left it. On a row with nothing to show the key does nothing rather than opening an empty panel — and the button is not drawn at all on a monitored bookmark still awaiting its first check.

Explained under Config → Help — Health & status now describes the enlarged view: what it shows, why it opens instantly, and why an empty window reads no data instead of 0%. There is a matching line in Tips & tricks, and the help filter finds both.

Outages always showed a length of "0s" — the outage list read the wrong field name for how long each one lasted, so every finished outage was reported as lasting no time at all. A twelve-minute outage now reads 12m. It was easy to overlook while outages only appeared inside the collapsed score panel; the enlarged view puts them in plain sight.
